shortExplanation: A kilometre is the largest of the listed unit lengths.
detailedSteps: In metres the lengths are $0.01$, $1000$, $0.001$, $1$ and $10^{-9}$. The largest is $1000\,\mathrm m$, or one kilometre.
keyIdeas: Express lengths in a common unit
commonMistakes: Comparing unit names without converting their prefixes.
difficultyNotes: This is a direct comparison after a unit conversion.

shortExplanation: Angles of incidence and reflection are equal, each measured from the mirror normal.
detailedSteps: At the point of incidence, draw a perpendicular to the sloping mirror. The reflected ray makes the same angle with that normal on its other side.
The resulting ray travels upward and to the right through the plotted point C.
commonMistakes: Reflecting the ray about a horizontal line instead of the actual mirror normal.
difficultyNotes: Use the actual drawn geometry to distinguish the candidate points.

shortExplanation: Multiply by seconds per week and divide by metres per mile.
detailedSteps: $$c\approx(3.0\times10^8)\frac{604800}{1609.344}\approx1.13\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{miles/week}.$$
commonMistakes: Dividing by the number of seconds in a week when converting a per-second speed to per-week.
difficultyNotes: Keep the direction of each conversion factor consistent.

shortExplanation: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency.
detailedSteps: $T=1/f=1/(2.00\,\mathrm{Hz})=0.50\,\mathrm s$. The printed wave speed would be needed for wavelength, not period.
commonMistakes: Using wave speed in a calculation that asks only for period.
difficultyNotes: Recognize which given quantity determines the requested result.

shortExplanation: Multiply the measured dimensions and round to three significant digits.
detailedSteps: The width and height each have three significant digits, so the product is reported as $3.79\times10^2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.
commonMistakes: Reporting every calculator digit as physically significant.
difficultyNotes: Retain extra digits during multiplication, then round once.

shortExplanation: A wavelength near 400 nanometres belongs to violet visible light.
detailedSteps: Violet occupies the short-wavelength end of the visible spectrum. Radio and microwave wavelengths are much longer, while X-rays are much shorter.
commonMistakes: Assigning a visible wavelength to X-rays simply because it is small.
difficultyNotes: This requires recognizing the order of electromagnetic wavelength ranges.

shortExplanation: The known mass and acceleration already determine the net force.
detailedSteps: $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma=(5.00)(2.00)=10.0\,\mathrm N$ to the right. Individual applied forces need not be specified to find their resultant.
keyIdeas: Net force equals mass times acceleration
commonMistakes: Assuming the net force cannot be found without listing every individual force.
difficultyNotes: Use the common conditions for this question and the following one.

shortExplanation: Relate the two speeds to displacement through the known acceleration.
commonMistakes: Subtracting the speeds before squaring instead of subtracting their squares.
difficultyNotes: The shared acceleration is constant, so this relation applies directly.

shortExplanation: Use the current-squared expression for resistive power.
commonMistakes: Dividing power by current only, which gives voltage.
difficultyNotes: Identify the formula that uses the two given electrical quantities.

shortExplanation: The tension is smaller than both the net-force magnitude and the weight.
detailedSteps: The weight is $G=Mg=100\,\mathrm N$, and the downward net force has magnitude $F=Ma=60\,\mathrm N$.
Taking upward as positive, $T-G=-Ma$, so $T=40\,\mathrm N$. Hence $T<F<G$.
commonMistakes: Adding tension and weight as though they point in the same direction.
difficultyNotes: Separate the net force from the two forces that produce it.

shortExplanation: The released mass continues along its instantaneous tangent.
detailedSteps: For the stated counterclockwise motion, the tangent at the upper-left point B points down and left through P.
The radius toward P is not the release direction; the mass does not acquire an outward radial velocity when the string is released.
commonMistakes: Releasing at the leftmost point merely because it is closest to P.
difficultyNotes: Read both the rotation direction and the tangent at each candidate point.

shortExplanation: Speed describes magnitude without direction.
detailedSteps: Impulse, momentum, acceleration and displacement are vectors. Speed is the scalar magnitude of velocity.
commonMistakes: Treating acceleration as scalar because it is often written as one number in a one-dimensional example.
difficultyNotes: Distinguish the physical quantity from a particular coordinate representation.

shortExplanation: Each removed electron increases the remaining net charge by one elementary charge.
commonMistakes: Multiplying by the elementary charge instead of dividing by it.
difficultyNotes: The positive sign comes from removing negative particles.

shortExplanation: The resistor next to the battery is in series with two equal parallel branches.
detailedSteps: The parallel pair has resistance $R/2$. Thus $R_{\mathrm{eq}}=R+R/2=3R/2$.
commonMistakes: Treating all three drawn resistors as a series chain.
difficultyNotes: Follow connections rather than the positions of components on the page.

shortExplanation: After first quarter, the visible illuminated part grows toward full Moon.
detailedSteps: That increasing, more-than-half illuminated phase is waxing gibbous. Waning gibbous occurs after the full Moon.
commonMistakes: Interchanging waxing and waning phases.
difficultyNotes: The sequence was checked against the primary NASA phase description.

shortExplanation: Use the angle between the applied force and the uphill displacement.
detailedSteps: The original diagram places the force $20^\circ$ above the incline. Therefore $$W_F=Fd\cos20^\circ=(50)(6.0)\cos20^\circ\approx282\,\mathrm J.$$
commonMistakes: Using the incline angle or including work by gravity in the requested applied-force work.
difficultyNotes: Read the marked force-displacement angle from the figure.

shortExplanation: Velocity is negative wherever the position graph slopes downward.
detailedSteps: The graph decreases from its maximum at 2.5 seconds to its minimum at 7.5 seconds. At those two turning times the tangent is horizontal, so the interval excludes its endpoints.
commonMistakes: Choosing the interval where position itself is negative.
difficultyNotes: Use the slope sign, not the height of the graph.

shortExplanation: Equal reaction forces need not perform equal work on bodies with different displacements.
detailedSteps: In the ordinary stationary-Earth approximation, the Earth hardly moves while the small object falls. Work on Earth is therefore represented by zero among the choices.
For a freely recoiling finite Earth, the work would instead be tiny and positive: in a two-body near-constant-force model, $W_{\mathrm{Earth}}/W_{\mathrm{object}}=m/M_{\mathrm{Earth}}$.
keyIdeas: Work depends on the displacement of the body acted on
commonMistakes: Assigning opposite work merely because the interaction forces are opposite.
difficultyNotes: The listed zero is the negligible-Earth-motion approximation, not an exact statement in every finite-mass or moving-frame model.

shortExplanation: For a fixed mass, kinetic energy is momentum magnitude squared divided by twice the mass.
keyIdeas: Kinetic energy in terms of momentum
commonMistakes: Using the square of the momentum change.
difficultyNotes: Only momentum magnitudes are needed; the given time interval is unnecessary.

shortExplanation: The position-momentum uncertainty relation is associated with Heisenberg.
detailedSteps: Position and its conjugate momentum have uncertainty widths constrained by $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\geq\hbar/2$. This is distinct from Pauli exclusion.
commonMistakes: Choosing Pauli because his principle also restricts quantum states.
difficultyNotes: This is a conceptual identification rather than a numerical uncertainty calculation.

finalAnswer: **It starts falling toward the ground** (choice A)
shortExplanation: An ordinary xenon-filled balloon is heavier than the air it displaces.
detailedSteps: At comparable ambient pressure and temperature, ideal-gas density is proportional to molar mass. Xenon has a molar mass about $131\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, much larger than air near $29\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.
Its gas weight plus the balloon envelope exceeds the buoyant force, so it begins falling after release.
commonMistakes: Assuming every gas-filled balloon rises like a helium balloon.
difficultyNotes: Use the ordinary ambient-temperature, near-ambient-pressure child’s-balloon model. An artificially heated xenon experiment would require additional thermal information.

shortExplanation: The net force points toward the circle center and has magnitude mass times radial acceleration.
detailedSteps: $$F_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{(4.0)(3.24)^2}{0.75}\approx56\,\mathrm N.$$
commonMistakes: Reporting the string tension, which also has to balance the downward weight.
difficultyNotes: The question asks for the resultant force, not a particular applied force.

shortExplanation: The equal-magnitude interaction forces give the lighter block the larger acceleration.
detailedSteps: At a time when the collision force has magnitude $F$, $a_1=F/3$ and $a_2=F/5$. Hence $a_1/a_2=5/3>1$.
commonMistakes: Inferring equal acceleration from equal and opposite forces.
difficultyNotes: The collision duration and energy loss do not affect this mass comparison.

shortExplanation: Take rightward velocity as positive before conserving momentum.
detailedSteps: The initial momentum is $3.00(-5.00)+5.00(2.00)=-5.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.
Afterward, $3.00(1.00)+5.00v_2=-5.00$, so $v_2=-1.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Its speed is $1.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
commonMistakes: Using the leftward initial speed as a positive velocity.
difficultyNotes: The collision need not conserve kinetic energy; total momentum is the relevant conserved quantity.

shortExplanation: The hour hand takes twelve hours for one full revolution.
detailedSteps: $$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{12(3600)}\approx1.45\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.$$
commonMistakes: Using the one-hour period of the minute hand.
difficultyNotes: Convert the full revolution time to seconds.

shortExplanation: Use the unchanged horizontal speed to obtain the final vertical component.
detailedSteps: The vertical speed at impact is $\sqrt{20.0^2-10.0^2}=10\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Since the initial vertical velocity is zero, $$t=\frac{10\sqrt3}{10}=\sqrt3\,\mathrm s\approx1.73\,\mathrm s.$$
commonMistakes: Treating the entire impact speed as vertical speed.
difficultyNotes: Resolve the final velocity before applying the vertical acceleration relation.

shortExplanation: Pressure is proportional to absolute temperature when volume and gas amount stay fixed.
detailedSteps: Then $T_{2K}=3(373.15)=1119.45\,\mathrm K$, giving $T_{2C}=1119.45-273.15=846.30\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$, represented by $846\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$.
commonMistakes: Tripling the Celsius temperature directly.
difficultyNotes: The listed answer is rounded; the precise Kelvin offset does not change its choice.

shortExplanation: An into-page conventional current produces clockwise magnetic-field circles.
detailedSteps: At a point directly to the right of the wire, the clockwise tangent points straight down. This is the straight arrow E, rather than one of the curved arrows.
keyIdeas: Local tangent of a circular field
commonMistakes: Choosing the curved path of a field line rather than its direction at P.
difficultyNotes: Apply the rule to the stated conventional current.

shortExplanation: Add the two lap times before dividing the total distance by total time.
detailedSteps: For lap length $d$, $$80=\frac{2d}{d/50+d/V}.$$ Thus $1/V=2/80-1/50=1/200$, giving $V=200\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
commonMistakes: Using the arithmetic mean of the two lap speeds.
difficultyNotes: The overall average weights each speed by its travel time.

shortExplanation: The sine in the bright-fringe condition cannot exceed one.
detailedSteps: From $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, the positive order satisfies $$m\leq\frac{42.4\,\mu\mathrm m}{550\,\mathrm{nm}}\approx77.09.$$ The greatest allowed integer is $77$.
commonMistakes: Rounding the order upward to a nonphysical fringe.
difficultyNotes: Use the full angular condition rather than a small-angle screen approximation.

shortExplanation: Include the energy of all three distinct charge pairs.
detailedSteps: The outer pair contributes $kQ^2/R$. Each outer-center pair contributes $kQQ_2/(R/2)$.
Therefore $$U=\frac{k}{R}(Q^2+4QQ_2)=0,$$ so $Q_2=-Q/4$ for the charged outer particles.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the interaction between the two outer charges.
difficultyNotes: No self energies are included, exactly as specified.

shortExplanation: The first physics Nobel Prize was awarded to Rontgen for X-rays.
detailedSteps: The first award was in 1901 and recognized Wilhelm Conrad Rontgen’s discovery of X-rays. Later neutron, radioactivity and photoelectric awards do not answer this historical question.
commonMistakes: Choosing a later prize recipient associated with another discovery.
difficultyNotes: The identity and discovery were checked against the primary Nobel account.

shortExplanation: The specified solid uniform sphere has rotational energy equal to two fifths of its translational energy.
detailedSteps: Using $I=2MR^2/5$ and $v=\omega R$, $$K_{\mathrm{rot}}=\frac12I\omega^2=\frac25\left(\frac12Mv^2\right).$$ Hence $K_{\mathrm{trans}}=(5/2)(20)=50\,\mathrm J$.
commonMistakes: Using the moment of inertia of a ring or disk.
difficultyNotes: The source explicitly specifies a uniform solid sphere and rolling without slipping.

shortExplanation: The weight has a horizontal lever arm because it acts vertically.
detailedSteps: The angle is measured below the horizontal, so the horizontal separation from pivot to mass is $L\cos\theta$. The torque magnitude is therefore $mgL\cos\theta$.
commonMistakes: Using a sine as though the angle were measured from vertical.
difficultyNotes: Check that the result is largest for a horizontal string and vanishes when it is vertical.

shortExplanation: A convex lens requires at least four focal lengths between a real object and its real image.
detailedSteps: For positive object and image distances, $pq=f(p+q)$. If $p+q=3f$, then $pq=3f^2$.
But $(p+q)^2\geq4pq$ would require $9f^2\geq12f^2$, which is impossible. No such real-image setup exists.
commonMistakes: Counting quadratic roots without checking that the requested real-image geometry is possible.
difficultyNotes: A domain check resolves the problem before solving for image distances.

finalAnswer: **Upward velocity and rightward magnetic field** (choice D)
shortExplanation: The magnetic force must point into the page to cancel the outward electric force.
detailedSteps: For a positive charge, $\mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$. Upward $\mathbf v$ crossed with rightward $\mathbf B$ points into the page.
The magnitudes can then satisfy $E=vB$. The other listed direction pairs cannot oppose the outward electric field.
keyIdeas: Constant velocity requires zero net force
commonMistakes: Reversing the magnetic force as though the moving charge were negative.
difficultyNotes: Check both the velocity and field directions in each table row.

shortExplanation: Compare the head area with the area occupied by one atom.
detailedSteps: The head area is about $\pi(0.005)^2\approx8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
An atomic spacing of a few $10^{-10}\,\mathrm m$ corresponds to an area near $10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ per atom, giving an atom count of order $10^{15}$.
commonMistakes: Counting the entire nail volume rather than its top monolayer.
difficultyNotes: This is an order estimate, not an exact lattice packing calculation.

finalAnswer: **The loop sides tend to move inward** (choice E)
shortExplanation: The induced current makes each side experience an inward magnetic force.
detailedSteps: An increasing into-page flux induces counterclockwise current. Crossing each directed current segment with the into-page magnetic field gives a force toward the loop interior.
Symmetry cancels net translation and torque, while the separate sides have a shrinking tendency.
commonMistakes: Predicting a net upward motion from only one side’s force.
difficultyNotes: Distinguish a tendency to deform from a net force on the whole loop.

shortExplanation: Closing the second branch doubles the load current needed for the same current in bulb 1.
detailedSteps: Let $b$ be either bulb resistance and $\mathcal E$ the battery emf. Before switching, $I_1=\mathcal E/(8+26+b)$.
After switching, equal bulbs share the total current, so $I_1'=\mathcal E/[2(8+R+b/2)]$.
Equal brightness requires equal bulb current: $2(8+R+b/2)=8+26+b$. Therefore $R=9.0\,\Omega$, independent of $b$.
keyIdeas: Same bulb current for same power
commonMistakes: Ignoring the battery’s internal resistance when changing the parallel load.
difficultyNotes: The unknown bulb resistance cancels only after the entire circuit is compared.

shortExplanation: Pressure times volume determines translational kinetic energy without requiring the molar mass.
detailedSteps: $PV=M_{\mathrm{gas}}v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/3$, so $$v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3(3.0)(101325)(6.0\times10^{-3})}{0.058}}\approx307\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$
commonMistakes: Using 58 grams as a molar mass or forgetting the litre conversion.
difficultyNotes: Keep total mass and volume in SI units.

finalAnswer: **Two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons** (choice C)
shortExplanation: An alpha particle carries two protons and two neutrons away.
detailedSteps: The daughter loses two units of proton number and four units of mass number, which means it also has two fewer neutrons.
commonMistakes: Interpreting the four-unit mass-number change as four lost protons.
difficultyNotes: Use the hypothetical source nuclides only as labels for the stated alpha process.

shortExplanation: Set the surviving fraction to one half in the exponential law.
detailedSteps: $e^{-\lambda t_{1/2}}=1/2$ gives $$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{20}\approx0.0347\,\mathrm s,$$ represented by $0.035\,\mathrm s$.
commonMistakes: Using the reciprocal decay constant, which is the mean lifetime.
difficultyNotes: The logarithmic factor distinguishes half-life from mean lifetime.

finalAnswer: **Translational equilibrium; rotation need not be in equilibrium** (choice B)
shortExplanation: A vanishing resultant force constrains translation but does not fix the resultant torque.
detailedSteps: Two equal and opposite forces applied at different heights can form a couple. Their net force is zero while their torques reinforce each other.
Thus translational equilibrium is guaranteed, while rotational or static equilibrium needs additional information.
commonMistakes: Assuming that canceling forces automatically cancel their moments.
difficultyNotes: A concrete force-couple counterexample rules out the stronger claims.

shortExplanation: Sum both heat-absorption steps and compare with the work input over the complete cycle.
detailedSteps: Use $P_0V_0$ as the energy unit. For a monatomic gas, $U=3PV/2$. Along $AB$, $\Delta U=3/2$ and $W=1$, so $Q=5/2$. Along $BC$, $\Delta U=3$ and $W=0$, so $Q=3$.
Along $CD$, $Q=-5$; along $DA$, $Q=-3/2$. The net work done by the gas is $-1$, so the required work input is $1$.
Total absorbed heat is $5/2+3=11/2$. Therefore $$\mathrm{COP}=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{absorbed}}}{W_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{11}{2}.$$
keyIdeas: First law on all four legs
commonMistakes: Counting heat absorption only on the constant-pressure leg.
difficultyNotes: This uses the source’s ideal cycle with total positive heat absorption; no unprovided fixed-temperature Carnot reservoirs are assumed.

shortExplanation: The atom receives momentum opposite the emitted photon.
detailedSteps: The photon momentum is $E_\gamma/c$. Thus $$v\approx\frac{E_\gamma}{Mc}=\frac{10.0(1.60\times10^{-19})}{(4.00\times10^{-26})(3.0\times10^8)}\approx0.133\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$
commonMistakes: Assigning the entire photon energy to the atom’s recoil kinetic energy.
difficultyNotes: The recoil speed is far below light speed, so the atom’s nonrelativistic momentum relation is sufficient.

shortExplanation: Cancel all length powers and leave the dimensions of time squared.
detailedSteps: $[\hbar]=\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$ and $[G]=\mathrm{m^3/(kg\,s^2)}$. Consequently $$[\hbar G/c^n]=\mathrm{m^{5-n}s^{n-3}}.$$ Matching time squared gives $n=5$.
keyIdeas: Track mass, length and time powers
commonMistakes: Forgetting that the given expression is for the square of Planck time.
difficultyNotes: Solve the unit exponents before substituting any physical constants.

shortExplanation: Account for both the speed increase and the rise in height.
detailedSteps: Continuity gives lower speed $v_L=(10.0/30.0)(9.0)=3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the height term or reversing its sign.
difficultyNotes: The narrowing and upward motion both reduce pressure at the upper section.

shortExplanation: The downward incoming and upward outgoing momenta add in the magnitude of the impulse.
detailedSteps: The incident speed is $\sqrt{2gH}$ and the rebound speed, from the rise to $H/2$, is $\sqrt{gH}$.
Taking upward as positive, $$|\Delta p|=M\bigl(\sqrt{gH}+\sqrt{2gH}\bigr).$$ Therefore $$|\overline F_{\mathrm{net}}|=(\sqrt2+1)\frac{M\sqrt{gH}}{T}.$$
commonMistakes: Subtracting the two speed magnitudes or reporting the contact force instead of net force.
difficultyNotes: An average contact-force answer would additionally include the weight; this question explicitly asks for net force.

shortExplanation: Complete polarization of the reflected beam identifies the Brewster angle.
detailedSteps: For light entering glass from air, $\tan\theta_B=n_{\mathrm{glass}}/n_{\mathrm{air}}$. Taking $n_{\mathrm{air}}\approx1$, $$n_{\mathrm{glass}}\approx\tan58^\circ\approx1.60.$$
commonMistakes: Using the complementary angle instead of the stated incidence angle.
difficultyNotes: Distinguish Brewster polarization from a total-internal-reflection condition.

shortExplanation: The decreasing outward electric field produces a clockwise magnetic field around the circular region.
detailedSteps: The electron is drawn outside the electric-field region, so the specified electric field gives it no direct electric force. The induced magnetic field at the point below the circle points left.
Upward velocity crossed with a leftward field points out of the page. Multiplying by the negative electron charge reverses the magnetic force into the page.
keyIdeas: Charge sign in the Lorentz force
commonMistakes: Applying the interior electric field at the outside electron or forgetting its negative charge.
difficultyNotes: Use the magnetic field induced by the changing electric flux and the actual electron location.
